entry.title: Working out a disagreement together
entry.summary: Describe the problem and leave space for your child’s idea. With a young toddler, you may supply most of the possibilities while they learn how it feels to work something out together.
entry.cue: Two people want different things, or the same difficulty keeps returning.
detail: Davies includes toddlers before fluent speech. If a crawling sibling takes a toy, her example is a toddler offering the sibling another toy to play with. A gesture or action can contribute; the adult still leads and keeps necessary limits.
Try a plan you can both live with and return to it if it is not working. A picture or brief note can also show that you heard a concern you cannot address just now.
The book’s notes are occasional aids. They do not replace the adult’s attention or the immediate action needed for safety.

references.locator: Adult leadership, preverbal participation, ideas and revisiting a plan
Moderate use of reminders and notebook acknowledgment

ageContext.bookAge: The problem-solving passage explicitly includes preverbal toddlers.
ageContext.readiness: A gesture or action may contribute; the adult may supply most ideas and retains safety responsibility.
ageContext.note: Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14.

displayContext.footer: You don’t need a different home. Start with what you have.
displayContext.colophon: Original summaries inspired by The Montessori Baby and The Montessori Toddler. Open any idea for its book references. The illustration is an invitation to explore, rather than a room to reproduce. Follow your child’s pace.
